title: SM wakeup lag + decoder-head imbalance — Nsight scan notes
content:
Quick summary:

What I saw in the November Nsight run (capture id above): a repeatable tail-latency mode when running the 8-head decoder microbatch workload. Average token time is fine, but p95/p99 spikes correlate with periods where a subset of SMs show long idle gaps between kernel waves — not simple occupancy shortage, but a wakeup latency pattern.

Observed evidence:
- Timeline: recurring ~1.2–6.8 ms gaps on 4–6 SMs while the rest are active; these gaps line up with kernel-queue submission boundaries from our CUDA graph replay.
- Kernel timing: attention-kernel (attn_v2) execution time is steady on active SMs but launch-to-start varies by 0.8–2.5 ms for affected blocks.
- CUDA graph notes: when using graph capture + external replays, we see batches that schedule a long chain of small kernels; some kernels are persistent-style long-running, others are micro kernels that rely on quick SM handoff. The handoff appears delayed for certain SMs.
- No obvious memory copy stalls (async memcpy streams show consistent throughput). L2/cache misses increase slightly on affected waves, but not enough to explain multi-ms gaps.

Hypothesis 1 — scheduler throttle / SM wakeup latency:
- When a wave finishes early on an SM, the SM goes idle and the hardware scheduler has to re-awaken it for the next kernel partition. Under certain kernel fragmentation patterns (many small kernels separated by work queues), wakeup latency becomes visible and varies SM-to-SM depending on prior occupancy/clock state.
- Evidence: affected SMs show a short period of reduced SM clock and lower issue rates before the next wave starts. This fits a hw power/clock ramp-up handoff rather than pure occupancy.

Hypothesis 2 — decoder-head imbalance + divergence in per-head workload:
- Decoder per-head sizes change across steps (due to sparse attention mask adaptation and head pruning heuristics). Some threadblocks are assigned more non-zero work and finish later, leaving partner blocks waiting. On GPU topologies where threadblocks map unevenly to SMs, this creates visible SM imbalance.
- Evidence: per-block active lane counts show heavier lane divergence in the attention gather stage for the same kernels when running the evaluation input set.

Short experiments run so far (quick/cheap):
1) Replayed same capture but forced single-stream replay (disable concurrent graph replays) — tail spikes reduced but not eliminated.
2) Increased microbatch size from 8 to 12 (fewer kernels overall) — p99 improved ~10% but avg token latency rose ~6% (tradeoff).
3) Inserted tiny dummy kernel (no-op) as a filler between attention and KV-update in capture — odd result: some captures got worse, others better depending on stream ordering. Shows sensitivity to kernel fragmentation.

Planned next experiments (priority order):
- Experiment A: persistent kernel prototype for the attention step (long-running block that pulls work from a global queue) to remove scheduling wakeups entirely. Measurement: p50/p95/p99 and SM idle histograms.
- Experiment B: adjust graph capture boundaries to coalesce small kernels where safe (reduce kernel-launch count). Check if coalescing reduces wakeup gaps.
- Experiment C: try setting stream priorities and explicit CUDA event ordering to see if scheduler/starvation semantics change behaviour under load.
- Experiment D: microarchitectural probe — use nvprof counters in targeted windows to confirm if SM clock scaling correlates with gaps (SMCLK, occupancy, issue_utilization).

Suggested mitigations (short list):
- For production: add fallbacks in router: when request length distribution is spiky, prefer larger microbatching or a variant model with fused attention kernels.
- Runtime: heuristics to detect kernel fragmentation pattern and either coalesce or switch to persistent kernels for the next N steps.
- Platform: explore using CUDA graph + persistent kernel hybrid: capture a persistent attention kernel inside a graph to preserve replays while reducing launches.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Is this specific to the Nvidia driver we used (525.x) — need to test on 530+ and older 470 series.
- Does this interact with GPU power-management settings at the host level (nvidia-smi application clocks, or host-level powertune)?
- Are certain SM indices systematically affected (topology mapping), or is it purely dynamic depending on prior wave timing?

Notes for reproducing quickly:
1) Use the provided capture id (linked_artifacts) and the small input set in /testdata/decoder/imbalance/input-variant-A.json.
2) Run 4 concurrent graph replays with microbatch=8, seq_len=1024 on a single A100.
3) Collect NVTX timeline and SM clock counters with 5 ms sampling windows.

Quick checklist for next run (assignments):
- Diego: prototype persistent attention kernel (two-phase: queue pop + compute) — target 2 weeks.
- Priya: run driver sweep across 470/525/530 and collect p99 telemetry — target 4 days.
- Liam: try coalescing capture boundaries in the replay harness and measure kernel launch count reduction — target 3 days.
- Me (Anika): correlate SM index mapping with threadblock ids from the last capture and produce an SM-mapping heatmap for the next sync.

Appendix (raw observations snippets):
- Timeline excerpt (SM 3): idle gap 3.1 ms between end-of-wave@T=334.7 ms and start@T=337.8 ms; preceding wave on SM 7 finished at 335.0 ms.
- Kernel list around gap: attn_v2 -> kv_update -> small_matmul -> attn_v2 (next step).
- Note: when kv_update is fused into attn_v2 in a quick A/B test build, gaps dropped by ~70% in that capture.

Conclusion (tl;dr):
We likely have a mix of SM wakeup latency (hardware scheduler / power/clock handoff) plus uneven per-head work distribution driving SM imbalance. Practical fixes: reduce kernel fragmentation (coalesce/fuse) or move to persistent kernels for the attention stage. Next runs: driver sweep + persistent kernel prototype + capture with coalesced kernels.
